How to read this report

Every result carries one of three labels. They tell you how much weight the result can bear.

Exploratory  Describes the data. No hypothesis was tested.

Statistically supported  Result of a formal test with error control, valid under the model's assumptions.

Biological interpretation  A hypothesis linking results to prior knowledge. Needs independent validation.

All numbers, tables and figures below were produced by the analysis run named above and are stored with it.

Summary

Kidney cancer lipids (Hakimi et al. 2016, 140 pairs), 280 samples was analysed with the Lipidomics workflow (version 1.0.0) on the LSMA Analysis Lab. To find which lipids differ between 'tumour' and 'normal' (column 'tissue'), adjusting for patient. In summary, 82 lipids passed the thresholds; the model reached Q2 = 0.841. 6 point(s) are flagged under Limitations and should be read before the results are used.

  • 82 lipids passed the thresholds.
  • The model reached Q2 = 0.841.

Introduction

From a table of lipid intensities to quality control, normalisation, the composition of the sample by lipid class, the length and saturation of the fatty-acid chains, and a per-lipid comparison between two groups. Lipids are named in the usual shorthand, so the structure of each molecule is read out of its name and analysed as well as its abundance. Peak picking and lipid identification from raw spectra happen before this workflow. The data analysed here is of kind 'lipid_table'.

Aim

To find which lipids differ between 'tumour' and 'normal' (column 'tissue'), adjusting for patient.

Methods

Assembled from what each completed stage recorded. Check it against the parameter tables below before using it in a write-up.

Lipid intensities were read from kidney_lipids.tsv: 107 lipid species in 280 study samples, 0 pooled QC samples and 0 blanks. Scale: raw intensities or concentrations; zeros were treated as not measured.

Of 280 uploaded samples, 280 took part in the comparison of 'tissue' (normal, tumour); 0 samples were excluded by the analyst for the reasons listed under Data input.

Quality control: lipids were kept when measured in at least 50% of the samples of at least one group of 'tissue', leaving 104 of 107.

Normalisation: probabilistic quotient normalisation: each sample is divided by the median of its ratios to a reference profile (the median of all study samples). Missing values (11% of the table): half of the smallest value measured for that lipid (for values below the detection limit). Intensities were log2-transformed.

Lipid class, chain length and number of double bonds were parsed from the species names in the shorthand notation of Liebisch et al.; 103 of 104 names could be read, giving 11 classes. Each class was expressed as a share of the total lipid signal per sample (sums taken on the linear scale) and compared between tumour against normal with Wilcoxon's test (pairing: paired by 'patient' over 140 pair(s)), corrected across classes with the Benjamini-Hochberg method at q < 0.05.

Chain length and saturation were summarised per sample as the abundance-weighted mean number of carbons and double bonds over the 103 species carrying chain information, together with the share of the signal from saturated, mono- or di-unsaturated and polyunsaturated species. The same measures were computed within each class of at least five species. All were compared between tumour against normal with Wilcoxon's test (pairing: paired by 'patient' over 140 pair(s)) and Benjamini-Hochberg correction.

Differential abundance of individual lipids was tested with limma (empirical Bayes moderated t-test) on log2 intensities using the design ~ patient + tissue for the contrast tumour vs normal. P-values were adjusted with the BH method; lipids with adjusted p-value below 0.05 and an absolute log2 fold change of at least 0 were called.

A multivariate model was fitted with OPLS-DA (ropls), pareto scaling, 7-fold cross-validation, 200 permutations: R2Y = 0.856, Q2 = 0.841, permutation p-value for Q2 = 0.005.

Random seed: 42. Software: R 4.5.2; Bioconductor 3.21; data.table 1.18.6.1; jsonlite 2.0.0; limma 3.64.3; ropls 1.40.0.

Analyses were run on the LSMA Analysis Lab (workflow 'lipidomics' version 1.0.0).

Results

One section per stage, in the order they ran. The badge on each heading says how far its output can be taken: exploratory output describes the data, statistically supported output carries a test, and interpretation is a reading of either.

Stage 1 of 8

Data input Exploratory

Lipidomics measures the fats of a sample: the phospholipids that make its membranes, the triacylglycerols it stores energy in, the sphingolipids it signals with, the cholesterol esters it ships cholesterol as. A mass spectrometer produces a signal for each, either after chromatography or by direct infusion ("shotgun" lipidomics), and software turns the spectra into a table with one number per lipid and sample. This stage reads that table whichever way round it is laid out, treats a zero as "not measured", and sorts the samples into study samples, pooled quality-control (QC) samples and blanks.

Note. No pooled QC samples were recognised. The reproducibility of each lipid over the run cannot be checked.

Sample preparation

Comparison: tissue, groups normal, tumour (reference: normal). Paired by patient. Adjusted for: patient. These choices were made before the analysis and the uploaded files were not changed.

No sample was excluded by the analyst.

Stage 2 of 8

Quality control and filtering Exploratory

Three filters, in order. A lipid missing from most samples of every group is dropped, because nothing can be said about it. A lipid that varies more than it should between repeated injections of the same pooled QC mixture is dropped, because that variation is the instrument's. A lipid no stronger in the samples than in the blanks is dropped, because it is background.

Note. Fewer than three pooled QC samples: lipids could not be filtered by reproducibility. Results for single lipids deserve more caution.

Stage 3 of 8

Normalisation Exploratory

Two samples can differ in total signal because one held more tissue, or was extracted more efficiently, or was injected when the instrument was more sensitive. Normalisation removes that. The values are then logged, which makes their spread roughly even across the range and turns a fold change into a difference.

Note. Normalisation factors differ 10.9-fold between samples. Samples that needed a very large correction were much more dilute; their weak lipids are less reliable.

Stage 5 of 8

Lipid classes Statistically supported

Every lipid name is taken apart into its class, the total carbons of its chains, its double bonds and any extra oxygens. The lipids are then added up by class, each class is expressed as a share of the sample's total lipid signal, and those shares are compared between the two groups with Wilcoxon's test.

Note. 1 of 104 row names (1%) could not be read as a lipid name and are counted under 'Other or unrecognised class'. They take no part in the chain-length and saturation stage.

How to interpret this stage

Read the composition bars first, then the table. The size of a class matters as much as its p-value, so a class holding a tenth of a percent of the signal can double without meaning much. A fall in membrane phospholipids with a rise in triacylglycerol is a tissue storing fat; a rise in lysophospholipids often means the sample was breaking down before it was frozen.

Stage 6 of 8

Chain length and saturation Statistically supported

Each sample gets two numbers: the average length of its fatty-acid chains and the average number of double bonds they carry, both weighted by how much of each lipid is present. The signal is also divided between saturated lipids, lipids with one or two double bonds, and polyunsaturated lipids with three or more. Every measure is compared between the groups, and then the same thing is done class by class.

Note. The lipids of 'tumour' are more saturated than those of 'normal' by 0.443 double bonds per lipid (q = 1.298e-21). This is a shift of the whole set, and says nothing about any single lipid.
Note. 1 lipid(s) carry no chain information in their name and are left out of this stage entirely.

How to interpret this stage

A shift of 0.2 double bonds per lipid is large. Check whether it happens inside the classes as well as between them. If every class moves the same way, the cause is which fatty acids the tissue had available; if only the storage lipids move, the cause is more likely what it chose to build.

Stage 8 of 8

PLS-DA model Statistically supported

PLS-DA looks for the combination of lipids that best separates the two groups. Because it is told the answer, it will always find something, so the model is judged by cross-validation (Q2, how well it predicts samples it was not fitted on) and by refitting it hundreds of times on shuffled group labels.

How to interpret this stage

R2Y says how much of the group difference the model captures; Q2 says how much it can predict. A large gap between them is overfitting. If the permutation test puts your model among the shuffled ones, there is no result here, whatever the score plot looks like.

Discussion

What the run amounts to, drawn from the stages that carry a judgement. Every sentence below was written by the stage that reached it; none is a later interpretation.

A share is a share of the signal measured, not a concentration. A method that sees phospholipids well and sterols badly will say so here.

Chain length and saturation are read from the lipid names. A name that gives only a total, such as 'PC 34:1', cannot say which of the two chains carries the double bond.

The run raised 6 warnings, listed with the stages that raised them. They are part of the result, not notes beside it.

Everything above was produced by Lipidomics on the data named in the Data section, with the parameters recorded under each stage. The Limitations section says what this design cannot show, and should be read before any of this is quoted.
